claim: Mature connective tissues demonstrate highly specialised properties, remarkably adapted to meet their functional requirements.
source: Mature connective tissues demonstrate highly specialised properties, remarkably adapted to meet their functional requirements.
evidence: This is a general statement about connective tissue properties presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this quote, but represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: Tissue adaptation to environmental cues can occur throughout life and poor adaptation commonly results in injury.
source: Tissue adaptation to environmental cues can occur throughout life and poor adaptation commonly results in injury.
evidence: This statement draws on established understanding in the field about tissue adaptation and injury risk.

claim: Adaptation in tendon occurs postnatally, following mechanical loading.
source: demonstrating adaptation occurs postnatally, following mechanical loading, and is almost exclusively localised to the non-collagenous interfascicular matrix.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript comparing foetal and postnatal samples.

claim: Adaptation in tendon is almost exclusively localised to the non-collagenous interfascicular matrix.
source: demonstrating adaptation occurs postnatally, following mechanical loading, and is almost exclusively localised to the non-collagenous interfascicular matrix.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the biomechanical, structural, and compositional data comparing fascicle and IFM across development.

claim: Poor tissue optimisation during maturation is likely a key contributor to increased injury risk later in life.
source: Adaptation to mechanical requirements is key in healthy development and homeostatic tissue maintenance, with poor tissue optimisation during maturation likely a key contributor to increased injury risk later in life.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between tissue development and injury susceptibility.

claim: Dysregulated homeostasis and long-term under- or over-stimulation leads to maladaptation, changes in tissue integrity, and reduced mechanical competence.
source: Dysregulated homeostasis and long-term under- or over-stimulation leads to maladaptation, changes in tissue integrity, and reduced mechanical competence and is implicated in the disease aetiology of load-bearing tissues (Freedman et al., 2015; Gardner et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Dysregulated homeostasis is implicated in the disease aetiology of load-bearing tissues.
source: Dysregulated homeostasis and long-term under- or over-stimulation leads to maladaptation, changes in tissue integrity, and reduced mechanical competence and is implicated in the disease aetiology of load-bearing tissues (Freedman et al., 2015; Gardner et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: There is currently little knowledge of the key extracellular matrix components associated with structural specialisation.
source: However, there is currently little knowledge of the key extracellular matrix (ECM) components associated with structural specialisation, the temporal nature of their adaptation, or the stimuli that drive adaptation.
evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that motivates the current study.

claim: Collagen expression at the gene and protein level has been the focus of the majority of studies in relation to loading.
source: As the principal structural component of connective tissues, collagen expression at the gene and protein level has been the focus of the majority of studies in relation to loading, with some studies reporting increases in collagen synthesis and others noting collagen degradation in response to loading, depending on the tissue function or tissue structure in different species (Choi et al., 2018; Magnusson and Kjaer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some studies report increases in collagen synthesis in response to loading.
source: As the principal structural component of connective tissues, collagen expression at the gene and protein level has been the focus of the majority of studies in relation to loading, with some studies reporting increases in collagen synthesis and others noting collagen degradation in response to loading, depending on the tissue function or tissue structure in different species (Choi et al., 2018; Magnusson and Kjaer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Some studies report collagen degradation in response to loading, depending on the tissue function or tissue structure in different species.
source: As the principal structural component of connective tissues, collagen expression at the gene and protein level has been the focus of the majority of studies in relation to loading, with some studies reporting increases in collagen synthesis and others noting collagen degradation in response to loading, depending on the tissue function or tissue structure in different species (Choi et al., 2018; Magnusson and Kjaer, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: In tendons, the collagen structural framework is the fascicles.
source: In tendons, this collagen structural framework is the fascicles and it is surrounded by the primarily non-collagenous and glycoprotein-rich components of the ECM, termed the interfascicular matrix (IFM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b; Armiento et al., 2018; Thorpe and Screen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to a figure.

claim: Fascicles are surrounded by the primarily non-collagenous and glycoprotein-rich components of the ECM, termed the interfascicular matrix (IFM).
source: In tendons, this collagen structural framework is the fascicles and it is surrounded by the primarily non-collagenous and glycoprotein-rich components of the ECM, termed the interfascicular matrix (IFM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b; Armiento et al., 2018; Thorpe and Screen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and a figure showing tendon structure.

claim: Tendon is a fibre composite material in which 'fascicle' and 'IFM' phases have different mechanical properties.
source: This distinction is important, as it describes a fibre composite material, in which 'fascicle' and 'IFM' phases have different mechanical properties, and overall tissue mechanical properties and function are governed by the interplay of these two phases.
evidence: This is based on established understanding of tendon structure and the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Overall tissue mechanical properties and function are governed by the interplay of fascicle and IFM phases.
source: This distinction is important, as it describes a fibre composite material, in which 'fascicle' and 'IFM' phases have different mechanical properties, and overall tissue mechanical properties and function are governed by the interplay of these two phases.
evidence: This is an inference based on composite material mechanics and the experimental data.

claim: Adaptation of the IFM phase to mechanical stimuli remains poorly defined.
source: Whilst fascicle and collagen adaptation has received some attention, adaptation of the IFM phase to mechanical stimuli remains poorly defined.
evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Studies investigating the mechanoresponsive nature of load-bearing tissues tend to restrict their focus to specific fibre or matrix components with no spatial distinction.
source: Indeed, it is notable that the numerous studies investigating the mechanoresponsive nature of load-bearing tissues tend to restrict their focus to specific fibre or matrix components with no spatial distinction, and also focus on a single element of either structural or mechanical adaptation, such that limited information is gained (Cherdchutham et al., 2001a; Choi et al., 2019; Mendias et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mature tendons can present structural and mechanical specialisms.
source: It is well-established that mature tendons can present structural and mechanical specialisms (Thorpe et al., 2015b; Thorpe et al., 2016a; Thorpe et al., 2016c) and be grouped into two clear functional groups; stiff positional tendons, such as the anterior tibialis tendon and the equine common digital extensor tendon (CDET), that simply connect muscle to bone to effectively position limbs, whilst elastic energy-storing tendons, such as the Achilles tendon and the equine superficial digital flexor tendon (SDFT), are further specialised to provide an energy storing function, increasing locomotor efficiency by stretching and storing energy which they return to the system on recoil (McNeill Alexander, 2002; Batson et al., 2003; Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe and Screen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Tendons can be grouped into two clear functional groups: stiff positional tendons and elastic energy-storing tendons.
source: It is well-established that mature tendons can present structural and mechanical specialisms (Thorpe et al., 2015b; Thorpe et al., 2016a; Thorpe et al., 2016c) and be grouped into two clear functional groups; stiff positional tendons, such as the anterior tibialis tendon and the equine common digital extensor tendon (CDET), that simply connect muscle to bone to effectively position limbs, whilst elastic energy-storing tendons, such as the Achilles tendon and the equine superficial digital flexor tendon (SDFT), are further specialised to provide an energy storing function, increasing locomotor efficiency by stretching and storing energy which they return to the system on recoil (McNeill Alexander, 2002; Batson et al., 2003; Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe and Screen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Positional tendons simply connect muscle to bone to effectively position limbs.
source: It is well-established that mature tendons can present structural and mechanical specialisms (Thorpe et al., 2015b; Thorpe et al., 2016a; Thorpe et al., 2016c) and be grouped into two clear functional groups; stiff positional tendons, such as the anterior tibialis tendon and the equine common digital extensor tendon (CDET), that simply connect muscle to bone to effectively position limbs, whilst elastic energy-storing tendons, such as the Achilles tendon and the equine superficial digital flexor tendon (SDFT), are further specialised to provide an energy storing function, increasing locomotor efficiency by stretching and storing energy which they return to the system on recoil (McNeill Alexander, 2002; Batson et al., 2003; Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe and Screen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Energy-storing tendons increase locomotor efficiency by stretching and storing energy which they return to the system on recoil.
source: It is well-established that mature tendons can present structural and mechanical specialisms (Thorpe et al., 2015b; Thorpe et al., 2016a; Thorpe et al., 2016c) and be grouped into two clear functional groups; stiff positional tendons, such as the anterior tibialis tendon and the equine common digital extensor tendon (CDET), that simply connect muscle to bone to effectively position limbs, whilst elastic energy-storing tendons, such as the Achilles tendon and the equine superficial digital flexor tendon (SDFT), are further specialised to provide an energy storing function, increasing locomotor efficiency by stretching and storing energy which they return to the system on recoil (McNeill Alexander, 2002; Batson et al., 2003; Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe and Screen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The simple aligned organisation of tendon means that fascicle and IFM phases are spatially distinct.
source: Further, the simple aligned organisation of tendon means that fascicle and IFM phases are spatially distinct, enabling structural and mechanical characterisation of each phase independently (Thorpe et al., 2012; Thorpe and Screen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations and is a key methodological advantage exploited in the study.

claim: The SDFT has been shown to be highly analogous to the human Achilles tendon in its capacity for energy storage, injury profile and extent of specialisation.
source: The SDFT has been shown to be highly analogous to the human Achilles tendon in its capacity for energy storage, injury profile and extent of specialisation and the anatomically opposing CDET is an example of a positional tendon, functionally comparable to the human anterior tibialis tendon (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a; Biewener, 1998; Patterson-Kane and Rich, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and a figure showing the anatomical location.

claim: The CDET is an example of a positional tendon, functionally comparable to the human anterior tibialis tendon.
source: The SDFT has been shown to be highly analogous to the human Achilles tendon in its capacity for energy storage, injury profile and extent of specialisation and the anatomically opposing CDET is an example of a positional tendon, functionally comparable to the human anterior tibialis tendon (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a; Biewener, 1998; Patterson-Kane and Rich, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations and a figure.

claim: A significant increase in fascicle yield and failure properties was evident when comparing embryonic fascicles to those acquired immediately at birth.
source: A significant increase in fascicle yield and failure properties was evident when comparing embryonic fascicles to those acquired immediately at birth (Figure 1h–i and e–g, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: There is minimal distinction in fascicle mechanics between functionally distinct tendons.
source: However, data indicate minimal distinction in fascicle mechanics between functionally distinct tendons (Figure 1e–i) and, significantly, no specialisation for energy storage in response to loading during postnatal development.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: There is no specialisation for energy storage in fascicle mechanics in response to loading during postnatal development.
source: However, data indicate minimal distinction in fascicle mechanics between functionally distinct tendons (Figure 1e–i) and, significantly, no specialisation for energy storage in response to loading during postnatal development.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by the biomechanical data in Figure 1.

claim: The failure properties of the IFM continued to alter throughout development with failure properties increasing markedly from 6 months onwards.
source: Contrasting with fascicle mechanics, the failure properties of the IFM continued to alter throughout development with failure properties increasing markedly from 6 months onwards (Figure 2e–g).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: An extended region of low stiffness at the start of the loading curve (extended toe region) is specific to the SDFT IFM pull to failure curve.
source: We also identify the emergence of an extended region of low stiffness at the start of the loading curve (i.e. an extended toe region) specific to the SDFT IFM pull to failure curve (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The SDFT IFM shows development of an overall greater capacity for extension.
source: This indicates less resistance to extension, and together with the concomitant increase in IFM yield force and extension at yield (Figure 2h–i), demonstrates development of an overall greater capacity for extension in the SDFT IFM behaviour.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biomechanical data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The IFM of the energy-storing SDFT became significantly less stiff than that of the positional CDET during the initial toe region of the loading curve as the tendon adapts.
source: A summary of these findings is achieved by plotting the amount of IFM extension at different percentages of failure force (Figure 2j–k), highlighting how the IFM of the energy-storing SDFT became significantly less stiff than that of the positional CDET during the initial toe region of the loading curve as the tendon adapts.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2j-k.

claim: IFM viscoelasticity significantly decreased with development specifically in the energy-storing SDFT.
source: The viscoelastic properties of the developing IFM also showed significant interactions between tendon type and development, with IFM viscoelasticity significantly decreasing with development specifically in the energy-storing SDFT (Figure 2a,c–d), resulting in specialisation towards a more energy efficient structure.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Decreased IFM viscoelasticity in the SDFT results in specialisation towards a more energy efficient structure.
source: The viscoelastic properties of the developing IFM also showed significant interactions between tendon type and development, with IFM viscoelasticity significantly decreasing with development specifically in the energy-storing SDFT (Figure 2a,c–d), resulting in specialisation towards a more energy efficient structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between viscoelasticity and energy efficiency.

claim: The energy-storing SDFT and positional CDET appeared histologically similar in the foetus.
source: The energy-storing SDFT and positional CDET appeared histologically similar in the foetus, in both instances showing surprisingly poor demarcation of the IFM, which only became structurally distinct after birth and the initiation of loading (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by histological images in Figure 3a.

claim: The IFM only became structurally distinct after birth and the initiation of loading.
source: The energy-storing SDFT and positional CDET appeared histologically similar in the foetus, in both instances showing surprisingly poor demarcation of the IFM, which only became structurally distinct after birth and the initiation of loading (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is supported by histological data in Figure 3a.

claim: Fascicle development was generally consistent in both tendon types with cellularity and crimp showing a reduction with development.
source: Fascicle development was generally consistent in both tendon types with cellularity and crimp showing a reduction with development, cells displaying more elongated nuclei, and collagen showing a more linear organisation (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, scoring criteria Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological scoring data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Fascicle cells display more elongated nuclei with development.
source: Fascicle development was generally consistent in both tendon types with cellularity and crimp showing a reduction with development, cells displaying more elongated nuclei, and collagen showing a more linear organisation (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, scoring criteria Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data.

claim: Fascicle collagen shows a more linear organisation with development.
source: Fascicle development was generally consistent in both tendon types with cellularity and crimp showing a reduction with development, cells displaying more elongated nuclei, and collagen showing a more linear organisation (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, scoring criteria Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data.

claim: Only the SDFT IFM showed an increase in cellularity following tendon loading.
source: In contrast, the IFM demonstrated divergence between tendon types with only the SDFT IFM showing an increase in cellularity following tendon loading and a retention of IFM width throughout development (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data in Figure 3.

claim: The SDFT IFM showed a retention of IFM width throughout development.
source: In contrast, the IFM demonstrated divergence between tendon types with only the SDFT IFM showing an increase in cellularity following tendon loading and a retention of IFM width throughout development (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data in Figure 3.

claim: The abundance of major ECM proteins was generally consistent across fascicle and IFM in the foetus.
source: The abundance of major ECM proteins was also generally consistent across fascicle and IFM in the foetus, with divergence of protein composition between phases only evident with further development (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: Divergence of protein composition between fascicle and IFM phases is only evident with further development.
source: The abundance of major ECM proteins was also generally consistent across fascicle and IFM in the foetus, with divergence of protein composition between phases only evident with further development (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: Adaptation was driven by changes in non-collagenous ECM components specifically.
source: Notably adaptation was driven by changes in non-collagenous ECM components specifically, levels of which reduced in the fascicles and increased dramatically in the IFM through postnatal development (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: Levels of non-collagenous ECM components reduced in the fascicles through postnatal development.
source: Notably adaptation was driven by changes in non-collagenous ECM components specifically, levels of which reduced in the fascicles and increased dramatically in the IFM through postnatal development (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: Levels of non-collagenous ECM components increased dramatically in the IFM through postnatal development.
source: Notably adaptation was driven by changes in non-collagenous ECM components specifically, levels of which reduced in the fascicles and increased dramatically in the IFM through postnatal development (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: PRG4 (lubricin) and TNC were predominantly found in the IFM of tendons.
source: Of particular note, we demonstrate PRG4 (commonly known as lubricin) and TNC were predominantly found in the IFM of tendons and showed sparse staining or were absent, respectively, from the fascicles.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: PRG4 showed sparse staining in the fascicles.
source: Of particular note, we demonstrate PRG4 (commonly known as lubricin) and TNC were predominantly found in the IFM of tendons and showed sparse staining or were absent, respectively, from the fascicles.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: TNC was absent from the fascicles.
source: Of particular note, we demonstrate PRG4 (commonly known as lubricin) and TNC were predominantly found in the IFM of tendons and showed sparse staining or were absent, respectively, from the fascicles.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: Elastin is preferentially localised to the IFM.
source: We also demonstrate that elastin is preferentially localised to the IFM with its abundance decreasing only in the CDET with development.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical and biochemical data in Figure 4.

claim: Elastin abundance decreases only in the CDET with development.
source: We also demonstrate that elastin is preferentially localised to the IFM with its abundance decreasing only in the CDET with development.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Histological and compositional changes manifest after birth and with the initiation of loading.
source: Furthermore, we show histological and compositional changes manifest after birth and with the initiation of loading, but that histological and compositional adaptation to loading then occurs over a period of months, involving both upregulation and downregulation of different histologic variables and ECM constituents.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Histological and compositional adaptation to loading occurs over a period of months.
source: Furthermore, we show histological and compositional changes manifest after birth and with the initiation of loading, but that histological and compositional adaptation to loading then occurs over a period of months, involving both upregulation and downregulation of different histologic variables and ECM constituents.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal data presented throughout the results.

claim: Adaptation to loading involves both upregulation and downregulation of different histologic variables and ECM constituents.
source: Furthermore, we show histological and compositional changes manifest after birth and with the initiation of loading, but that histological and compositional adaptation to loading then occurs over a period of months, involving both upregulation and downregulation of different histologic variables and ECM constituents.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing increases and decreases in different components.

claim: The proteomic profile of the IFM was more complex (more identified proteins) than the fascicle.
source: Our results demonstrated that the proteomic profile of the IFM was more complex (more identified proteins) and a higher percentage of IFM proteins were cellular (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), supporting the histological findings of a more cellular IFM.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A higher percentage of IFM proteins were cellular.
source: Our results demonstrated that the proteomic profile of the IFM was more complex (more identified proteins) and a higher percentage of IFM proteins were cellular (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), supporting the histological findings of a more cellular IFM.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The IFM and fascicle had 14 collagens and 11 proteoglycans in common.
source: Notably, despite the two phases being structurally distinct, they had 14 collagens and 11 proteoglycans in common (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data in Supplementary file 4.

claim: Alterations in the fascicle proteome reduced through development, with minimal changes following the initiation of loading.
source: Overall, proteomic heatmap analysis correlated very strongly with immunohistochemical findings, showing that alterations in the fascicle proteome reduced through development, with minimal changes following the initiation of loading (Tables 1 and 2, Figure 5a), whilst numerous matrisome and matrisome-related proteins progressively increase in abundance through development in the IFM (Tables 1 and 2, Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data in Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 5a.

claim: Numerous matrisome and matrisome-related proteins progressively increase in abundance through development in the IFM.
source: Overall, proteomic heatmap analysis correlated very strongly with immunohistochemical findings, showing that alterations in the fascicle proteome reduced through development, with minimal changes following the initiation of loading (Tables 1 and 2, Figure 5a), whilst numerous matrisome and matrisome-related proteins progressively increase in abundance through development in the IFM (Tables 1 and 2, Figure 5a).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data in Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 5a.

claim: Post loading changes in the IFM appear more specific to proteoglycans and glycoproteins.
source: Detailed consideration of protein changes also highlights that post loading changes in the IFM appear more specific to proteoglycans and glycoproteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data in Tables 1 and 2.

claim: There is a negative correlation between proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP and COL3A1 and the IFM hysteresis.
source: Significant correlations included a negative correlation between proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP and COL3A1 and the IFM hysteresis, a positive correlation between FBLN5 and stress relaxation, a positive correlation between COL6A1, COL6A2, and OGN and maximum stiffness, and for the yield properties a positive correlation of proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP, and COL3A1 and force at yield point (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: There is a positive correlation between FBLN5 and stress relaxation.
source: Significant correlations included a negative correlation between proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP and COL3A1 and the IFM hysteresis, a positive correlation between FBLN5 and stress relaxation, a positive correlation between COL6A1, COL6A2, and OGN and maximum stiffness, and for the yield properties a positive correlation of proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP, and COL3A1 and force at yield point (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: There is a positive correlation between COL6A1, COL6A2, and OGN and maximum stiffness.
source: Significant correlations included a negative correlation between proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP and COL3A1 and the IFM hysteresis, a positive correlation between FBLN5 and stress relaxation, a positive correlation between COL6A1, COL6A2, and OGN and maximum stiffness, and for the yield properties a positive correlation of proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP, and COL3A1 and force at yield point (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: There is a positive correlation of proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP, and COL3A1 and force at yield point.
source: Significant correlations included a negative correlation between proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP and COL3A1 and the IFM hysteresis, a positive correlation between FBLN5 and stress relaxation, a positive correlation between COL6A1, COL6A2, and OGN and maximum stiffness, and for the yield properties a positive correlation of proteoglycans DCN, LUM, OGN, PRELP, and COL3A1 and force at yield point (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data in Supplementary file 5.

claim: Protein abundance for BGN, DCN, COMP, COL1A2, COL3A1 in the IFM across development is mirrored by whole tendon mRNA expression.
source: In addition, protein abundance for BGN, DCN, COMP, COL1A2, COL3A1 in the IFM and COMP and COL3A1 in the fascicles across development is mirrored by whole tendon mRNA expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Protein abundance for COMP and COL3A1 in the fascicles across development is mirrored by whole tendon mRNA expression.
source: In addition, protein abundance for BGN, DCN, COMP, COL1A2, COL3A1 in the IFM and COMP and COL3A1 in the fascicles across development is mirrored by whole tendon mRNA expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both fascicle and IFM phases display turnover during development.
source: In the current study, we were able to profile the temporal nature of fascicle and IFM turnover, demonstrating that both phases display turnover during development but that fascicle turnover slows down towards the end of maturation, whilst IFM turnover rates are maintained, suggesting structural and/or compositional plasticity (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by neopeptide data in Figure 5b.

claim: Fascicle turnover slows down towards the end of maturation.
source: In the current study, we were able to profile the temporal nature of fascicle and IFM turnover, demonstrating that both phases display turnover during development but that fascicle turnover slows down towards the end of maturation, whilst IFM turnover rates are maintained, suggesting structural and/or compositional plasticity (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by neopeptide data in Figure 5b.

claim: IFM turnover rates are maintained during development, suggesting structural and/or compositional plasticity.
source: In the current study, we were able to profile the temporal nature of fascicle and IFM turnover, demonstrating that both phases display turnover during development but that fascicle turnover slows down towards the end of maturation, whilst IFM turnover rates are maintained, suggesting structural and/or compositional plasticity (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is supported by neopeptide data in Figure 5b and represents an inference about plasticity.

claim: The canonical pathways 'integrin signalling' and 'actin cytoskeleton signalling' were predicted to be activated with development in the IFM.
source: Pathway analysis revealed the canonical pathways 'integrin signalling' and 'actin cytoskeleton signalling' were predicted to be activated with development in the IFM supporting an ECM-integrin-cytoskeleton to nucleus signalling pathway for the mediation of the observed mitogenesis and matrigenesis in response to tendon loading.
evidence: This is based on pathway analysis of the proteomic data using IPA software.

claim: An ECM-integrin-cytoskeleton to nucleus signalling pathway mediates the observed mitogenesis and matrigenesis in response to tendon loading.
source: Pathway analysis revealed the canonical pathways 'integrin signalling' and 'actin cytoskeleton signalling' were predicted to be activated with development in the IFM supporting an ECM-integrin-cytoskeleton to nucleus signalling pathway for the mediation of the observed mitogenesis and matrigenesis in response to tendon loading.
evidence: This is an inference based on pathway analysis.

claim: TGFB1 was identified as an upstream regulator for the IFM dataset.
source: In addition, pathway analysis identified TGFB1 as an upstream regulator for the IFM dataset and based on the IFM protein abundance across age groups predicted TGFB1 to be inhibited in the foetus age group and to become activated in the 3–6 months age group.
evidence: This is based on pathway analysis of the proteomic data.

claim: TGFB1 is predicted to be inhibited in the foetus age group.
source: In addition, pathway analysis identified TGFB1 as an upstream regulator for the IFM dataset and based on the IFM protein abundance across age groups predicted TGFB1 to be inhibited in the foetus age group and to become activated in the 3–6 months age group.
evidence: This is a prediction based on pathway analysis.

claim: TGFB1 is predicted to become activated in the 3–6 months age group.
source: In addition, pathway analysis identified TGFB1 as an upstream regulator for the IFM dataset and based on the IFM protein abundance across age groups predicted TGFB1 to be inhibited in the foetus age group and to become activated in the 3–6 months age group.
evidence: This is a prediction based on pathway analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: TGF-β1 is predicted to be upregulated in the energy-storing tendon following loading.
source: TGF-β1 was therefore highlighted as a potential regulator of ECM organisation and functional adaptation, predicted to be upregulated in the energy-storing tendon following loading (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a prediction based on pathway analysis shown in Figure 6a.

claim: TGFB1 mRNA expression increases in the 3–6 months SDFT only.
source: This was supported by TGB1 mRNA expression in whole tendon increasing in the 3–6 months SDFT only, with the positional CDET TGFB1 expression showing no change with development (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by mRNA expression data in Figure 6b.

claim: The positional CDET TGFB1 expression shows no change with development.
source: This was supported by TGB1 mRNA expression in whole tendon increasing in the 3–6 months SDFT only, with the positional CDET TGFB1 expression showing no change with development (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is supported by mRNA expression data in Figure 6b.

claim: Knockdown of TGFB1 in equine adult tenocytes showed downregulation of key ECM components BGN, COMP, COL1A2, and COL3A1.
source: In addition, knockdown of TGFB1 in equine adult tenocytes and stimulation with 10 ng recombinant TGF-β1 showed downregulation and upregulation, respectively, of key ECM components, BGN, COMP, COL1A2, and COL3A1, supporting a regulatory role for TGF-β1 (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6c.

claim: Stimulation with 10 ng recombinant TGF-β1 showed upregulation of key ECM components BGN, COMP, COL1A2, and COL3A1.
source: In addition, knockdown of TGFB1 in equine adult tenocytes and stimulation with 10 ng recombinant TGF-β1 showed downregulation and upregulation, respectively, of key ECM components, BGN, COMP, COL1A2, and COL3A1, supporting a regulatory role for TGF-β1 (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6d.

claim: TGF-β1 has a regulatory role for ECM components.
source: In addition, knockdown of TGFB1 in equine adult tenocytes and stimulation with 10 ng recombinant TGF-β1 showed downregulation and upregulation, respectively, of key ECM components, BGN, COMP, COL1A2, and COL3A1, supporting a regulatory role for TGF-β1 (Figure 6c–d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the knockdown and stimulation experiments.

claim: TGFB1 mRNA expression shows positive correlations with IFM matrisome protein abundance across development that are significant for COL1A2, COL2A1, COL4A1, COL4A2, COL6A3, HSPG2, and FN1.
source: Finally, correlation analysis of TGFB1 mRNA expression of whole tendon and IFM matrisome protein abundance across development revealed positive correlations with ECM proteins which were significant for COL1A2, COL2A1, COL4A1, COL4A2, COL6A3, HSPG2, and FN1 (Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis data in Supplementary file 6.

claim: The energy-storing SDFT undergoes peak strains recorded at 16.6% in vivo.
source: The energy-storing SDFT, which functions by stretching and recoiling with each stride to store and return energy, undergoes peaks strains recorded at 16.6% in vivo and has been found to be significantly more extensible than the CDET.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the discussion section.

claim: The SDFT has been found to be significantly more extensible than the CDET.
source: The energy-storing SDFT, which functions by stretching and recoiling with each stride to store and return energy, undergoes peaks strains recorded at 16.6% in vivo and has been found to be significantly more extensible than the CDET.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the discussion section.

claim: The positional CDET experiences much lower strains than the SDFT (estimated at 2.5%).
source: The positional CDET, which functions to extend the distal limb prior to limb placement and is relatively inextensible to allow precise placement of the limb, experiences much lower strains than the SDFT (estimated at 2.5%) and is less extensible than the SDFT (Batson et al., 2003; Birch et al., 2008; Thorpe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The CDET is less extensible than the SDFT.
source: The positional CDET, which functions to extend the distal limb prior to limb placement and is relatively inextensible to allow precise placement of the limb, experiences much lower strains than the SDFT (estimated at 2.5%) and is less extensible than the SDFT (Batson et al., 2003; Birch et al., 2008; Thorpe et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Limited previously available data on the development of tendon gross mechanical properties show an increase in mechanical properties with development.
source: Whilst the limited previously available data on the development of tendon gross mechanical properties show an increase in mechanical properties with development (Ansorge et al., 2011; Cherdchutham et al., 2001b), no such phase-specific analysis of the development of tissue mechanics has been carried out previously.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: No phase-specific analysis of the development of tissue mechanics has been carried out previously.
source: Whilst the limited previously available data on the development of tendon gross mechanical properties show an increase in mechanical properties with development (Ansorge et al., 2011; Cherdchutham et al., 2001b), no such phase-specific analysis of the development of tissue mechanics has been carried out previously.
evidence: This represents a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Available research into tendon morphogenesis and maturation has previously focused on the development of the collagenous network that comprises the tendon fascicles.
source: Similarly, available research into tendon morphogenesis and maturation has previously focused on the development of the collagenous network that comprises the tendon fascicles and is often focussed on early foetal development (Kalson et al., 2011; Marturano et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Murine and zebrafish models used to investigate tendon development lack an IFM.
source: Murine and zebrafish models used to investigate tendon development and adaptation have advanced our understanding of the control of fibrillogenesis by ECM proteins (Subramanian et al., 2018; Subramanian and Schilling, 2014; Taye et al., 2020), but these models lack an IFM, thus restricting our ability to explore the functional specialism we see in humans and other larger mammals.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents a limitation of these models.

claim: The low stiffness behaviour of the IFM allows sliding between the fascicles, enabling non-uniform loading of tissue and is fundamental for effective extension and recoil in energy-storing tendons.
source: We have previously indicated that this low stiffness behaviour allows sliding between the fascicles, enabling non-uniform loading of tissue and is fundamental for effective extension and recoil in energy-storing tendons (Thorpe et al., 2015b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: With ageing the low stiffness behaviour of the energy-storing IFM is lost, possibly contributing to disease development.
source: Furthermore, with ageing the low stiffness behaviour of the energy-storing IFM is lost, possibly contributing to disease development (Thorpe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents speculation about disease.

claim: Foetal and early postnatal tendons are highly cellular.
source: It is well recognised that foetal and early postnatal tendons are highly cellular, and cellularity is generally considered to decrease postnatally (Russo et al., 2015; Stanley et al., 2008), but here we show that the described reduction in cellularity only occurs in the fascicles, and cellularity in fact increases in the IFM with development.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Cellularity is generally considered to decrease postnatally in tendons.
source: It is well recognised that foetal and early postnatal tendons are highly cellular, and cellularity is generally considered to decrease postnatally (Russo et al., 2015; Stanley et al., 2008), but here we show that the described reduction in cellularity only occurs in the fascicles, and cellularity in fact increases in the IFM with development.
evidence: This is supported by citations but is contrasted with the current findings.

claim: The reduction in cellularity only occurs in the fascicles.
source: It is well recognised that foetal and early postnatal tendons are highly cellular, and cellularity is generally considered to decrease postnatally (Russo et al., 2015; Stanley et al., 2008), but here we show that the described reduction in cellularity only occurs in the fascicles, and cellularity in fact increases in the IFM with development.
evidence: This is a key finding from the histological data.

claim: Cellularity in fact increases in the IFM with development.
source: It is well recognised that foetal and early postnatal tendons are highly cellular, and cellularity is generally considered to decrease postnatally (Russo et al., 2015; Stanley et al., 2008), but here we show that the described reduction in cellularity only occurs in the fascicles, and cellularity in fact increases in the IFM with development.
evidence: This is a key finding from the histological data.

claim: The marked difference in regional cellularity is likely driven by a maintenance of cell numbers following tendon loading in the thinning IFM, while cell numbers in the fascicle appear to reduce as a result of the fascicle ECM increase.
source: By following the alterations in cellularity across IFM and fascicle, here we can determine that the marked difference in regional cellularity is likely driven by a maintenance of cell numbers following tendon loading in the thinning IFM, while cell numbers in the fascicle appear to reduce as a result of the fascicle ECM increase.
evidence: This is an inference based on the histological observations.

claim: Greater cellularity is commonly associated with a requirement for rapid adaptive organisation of ECM components.
source: Greater cellularity is commonly associated with a requirement for rapid adaptive organisation of ECM components (Russo et al., 2015), suggesting the IFM, particularly in the energy-storing tendons, may adapt to be more mechanoresponsive, a necessary aspect of healthy homeostatic maintenance of a tissue.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: The IFM, particularly in the energy-storing tendons, may adapt to be more mechanoresponsive.
source: Greater cellularity is commonly associated with a requirement for rapid adaptive organisation of ECM components (Russo et al., 2015), suggesting the IFM, particularly in the energy-storing tendons, may adapt to be more mechanoresponsive, a necessary aspect of healthy homeostatic maintenance of a tissue.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cellularity findings.

claim: Lubricin facilitates interfascicular sliding.
source: Using a lubricin-knockout mouse, this proteoglycan has been demonstrated to facilitate interfascicular sliding (Kohrs et al., 2011), indicating that this structural adaptation may be key in achieving the previously identified mechanical adaptation in the energy-storing tendon IFM.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: PRG4 expression and elastin expression decreased with ageing in rat tendon.
source: In addition, Kostrominova and Brooks, 2013 (Kostrominova and Brooks, 2013) report PRG4 expression as wells as elastin expression decreased with ageing in rat tendon suggesting an association with an increased risk of disease with ageing.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Decreased PRG4 and elastin expression with ageing suggests an association with an increased risk of disease with ageing.
source: In addition, Kostrominova and Brooks, 2013 (Kostrominova and Brooks, 2013) report PRG4 expression as wells as elastin expression decreased with ageing in rat tendon suggesting an association with an increased risk of disease with ageing.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cited work.

claim: Elastin has a role in the capacity for matrix recoil after loading which is necessary for the healthy function of energy-storing tendons.
source: We also demonstrate that elastin is preferentially localised to the IFM, potentially having a role in the capacity for matrix recoil after loading which is necessary for the healthy function of energy-storing tendons (Godinho et al., 2017; Ritty et al., 2002).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations.

claim: Elastin appears to be redundant in positional tendons.
source: Further supporting a role for elastin in the energy-storing function, elastin appears to be redundant in positional tendons with its abundance decreasing in the CDET with development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the elastin data.

claim: Once a tendon is mature, little collagen turnover occurs.
source: Once a tendon is mature, little collagen turnover occurs (Birch, 2007; Heinemeier et al., 2013) and we have previously shown that the minimal turnover in mature tendon is focused to the IFM (Choi et al., 2020; Thorpe et al., 2010; Thorpe et al., 2015a; Thorpe et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The minimal turnover in mature tendon is focused to the IFM.
source: Once a tendon is mature, little collagen turnover occurs (Birch, 2007; Heinemeier et al., 2013) and we have previously shown that the minimal turnover in mature tendon is focused to the IFM (Choi et al., 2020; Thorpe et al., 2010; Thorpe et al., 2015a; Thorpe et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Biomaterial and regenerative medicine studies have placed considerable emphasis on the fascicle region.
source: With the fascicles primarily responsible for the mechanical strength of a tissue, biomaterial and regenerative medicine studies have unsurprisingly placed considerable emphasis on this region to date (Sensini et al., 2019; Watts et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The IFM must be targeted to support adaptation and optimum tissue quality.
source: Here, we not only highlight the importance of the IFM in modulating mechanical behaviour, but also demonstrate how the IFM must be targeted to support adaptation and optimum tissue quality.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: TGF-β is a known regulator of proteoglycans and collagens in tendon.
source: TGF-β is a known regulator of proteoglycans and collagens in tendon (Potter et al., 2017; Robbins et al., 1997), a role we also demonstrated here with regulation of major ECM proteins mRNA expression following TGFB1 knockdown and stimulation in equine tenocytes.
evidence: This is supported by citations and the experimental data.

claim: TGFB1 mRNA expression was upregulated in the highly loaded energy-storing tendon only.
source: Further, TGFB1 mRNA expression was upregulated in the highly loaded energy-storing tendon only, supporting the hypothesis that TGF-β1 regulation is specific to the energy-storing tendon and subsequently indicating that it may specifically be associated with loading.
evidence: This is supported by the mRNA expression data.

claim: TGF-β1 regulation is specific to the energy-storing tendon.
source: Further, TGFB1 mRNA expression was upregulated in the highly loaded energy-storing tendon only, supporting the hypothesis that TGF-β1 regulation is specific to the energy-storing tendon and subsequently indicating that it may specifically be associated with loading.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mRNA expression data.

claim: TGF-β1 may specifically be associated with loading.
source: Further, TGFB1 mRNA expression was upregulated in the highly loaded energy-storing tendon only, supporting the hypothesis that TGF-β1 regulation is specific to the energy-storing tendon and subsequently indicating that it may specifically be associated with loading.
evidence: This is speculation based on the data.

claim: The divergence in mechanical properties, adaptation, and TGF-β regulation all occurs only in the tendon experiencing significant loading.
source: Whilst we acknowledge that other extrinsic factors may drive the changes, our direct comparison of the highly loaded SDFT with the low load CDET enables us to identify that the divergence in mechanical properties, adaptation, and TGF-β regulation all occurs only in the tendon experiencing significant loading.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative data.

claim: TGF-β has a role in cellular mechanobiology and connective tissue homeostasis, regulating ECM synthesis and remodelling in a force-dependent way following mechanical stimulation.
source: In addition, TGF-β has been shown to have a role in cellular mechanobiology and connective tissue homeostasis, regulating ECM synthesis and remodelling in a force-dependent way following mechanical stimulation, to specify the quality of the ECM and help coordinate cytoskeletal tension (Maeda et al., 2011; Subramanian et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: A previous study of developing chick tendon detected TGF-β1 staining in the IFM only, during development.
source: A previous study of developing chick tendon detected TGF-β1 staining in the IFM only, during development, highlighting its localised distribution in development (Kuo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: TGF-β1 is involved in connective tissue injury and repair with abnormal expression levels reported in both processes.
source: In addition to tissue development and homeostasis, TGF-β1 is involved in connective tissue injury and repair with abnormal expression levels reported in both processes suggesting a pleiotropic mode of action (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: TGF-β1 has a pleiotropic mode of action.
source: In addition to tissue development and homeostasis, TGF-β1 is involved in connective tissue injury and repair with abnormal expression levels reported in both processes suggesting a pleiotropic mode of action (Gao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation based on the cited work.

claim: TGF-β1 has a role in tissue development and homeostasis and its dysregulation is associated with tissue injury and repair.
source: The above may suggest a role for TGF-β1 in tissue development and homeostasis and that its dysregulation is associated with tissue injury and repair.
evidence: This is speculation based on the discussion.

claim: Functional adaptation in tendon is predominantly reliant on adaptation of the metabolically active IFM.
source: We demonstrate for the first time that functional adaptation in tendon is predominantly reliant on adaptation of the metabolically active IFM, which responds to the mechanical environment through TGF-β signalling, resulting in modulations in ECM turnover and composition to fine-tune mechanical properties.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion based on all the data presented.

claim: The IFM responds to the mechanical environment through TGF-β signalling.
source: We demonstrate for the first time that functional adaptation in tendon is predominantly reliant on adaptation of the metabolically active IFM, which responds to the mechanical environment through TGF-β signalling, resulting in modulations in ECM turnover and composition to fine-tune mechanical properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the TGF-β data and pathway analysis.

claim: TGF-β signalling results in modulations in ECM turnover and composition to fine-tune mechanical properties.
source: We demonstrate for the first time that functional adaptation in tendon is predominantly reliant on adaptation of the metabolically active IFM, which responds to the mechanical environment through TGF-β signalling, resulting in modulations in ECM turnover and composition to fine-tune mechanical properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the integrated findings.

claim: Regenerative medicine, biomimetics and biomechanics studies have largely focused on investigating and recapitulating the organisation and mechanical properties of the collagenous fibrous network.
source: Traditionally, the non-collagenous matrix phase of connective tissues has received considerably less attention than the fibre phase, with regenerative medicine, biomimetics and biomechanics studies all largely focused on investigating and recapitulating the organisation and mechanical properties of the collagenous fibrous network.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the field.

claim: Following tendon injury, normal tissue architecture is not recovered.
source: Following tendon injury, normal tissue architecture is not recovered, and in particular, the cellular IFM is not regenerated.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about tendon healing.

claim: The cellular IFM is not regenerated following tendon injury.
source: Following tendon injury, normal tissue architecture is not recovered, and in particular, the cellular IFM is not regenerated.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about tendon healing.

claim: Regeneration of the IFM following tendon injury could be key for tendon health and low re-injury risk.
source: Regeneration of the IFM following tendon injury could be key for tendon health and low re-injury risk.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings of the study.
